newsitem.title: GERMANY: German state grants reprieve for British cattle.
newsitem.headline: German state grants reprieve for British cattle.

text.p: The German state of Lower Saxony on Monday suspended the slaughter of cattle believed to represent a risk of mad cow disease after a court granted a temporary injunction.

The higher administrative court in Lueneburg ruled there was no need to circumvent usual procedures because all cows imported from Britain, where the disease is widespread, had been registered and could not be slaughtered for meat or sold.

Germany's federal and state agriculture ministries had agreed to slaughter over 5,000 cattle from Britain and Switzerland, the other country with a large number of cases of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), after a calf in Germany was found to have the disease.

Experts believe the disease may be transmissible to humans. Beef consumption in Germany has plunged as a result of the scare, and the slaughter was one of a number of measures intended to restore consumer confidence.
After the Lueneburg ruling, Lower Saxony Agriculture Minister Karl-Heinz Funke said the slaughter would be suspended in his state. Other states appeared likely to follow suit.
The standard procedure for ordering a slaughter of farm animals requires a decision by the Upper House (Bundesrat), where the 16 federal states are represented.

German farmers with livestock imported from Britain say there is no evidence their cattle are at risk since they were imported from BSE-free herds and because German farmers do not use the protein feed which is the main route of BSE transmission.
The calf at the centre of the latest scare is Germany's fifth BSE case in all. Experts have yet to establish whether the cow was a direct import, or born here to a cow imported from Britain.
